There’s a strange pleasure in writing without a destination. No outline. No thesis. No hidden agenda except the desire to see where the words happen to go. I think we don’t do enough of that—not just in writing, but in thinking itself. We’re always optimizing. We plan the day, schedule the meetings, structure the argument, and curate the feed until every corner of consciousness feels like a productivity dashboard. And yet some of the best ideas arrive exactly when we stop trying to arrive anywhere.

That’s what free writing feels like to me: a slow walk in a city you don’t know. You take a street because it’s shaded, not because it’s on the map. You stop because a baker’s window smells like butter, not because you were hungry. You notice that a particular doorway is painted a shade of blue you’ve never seen before, and suddenly you’re wondering who chose that color, and what they were thinking on the morning they picked it, and whether they ever regret it. That’s the beauty of an unconstrained mind—it doesn’t just follow a path; it makes paths, then abandons them, then makes others.

In a way, the models we build here remind me of that. Diffusion models don’t rewrite one word at a time like a cautious editor. They start with noise—a kind of beautiful chaos—and gradually refine it into something coherent. But during that refinement, many possibilities exist at once. The model isn’t locked into a single sentence from the first token. It holds a cloud of potential continuations, and only slowly does that cloud condense into language. I like to imagine those intermediate states as a writer’s draft before the inner critic shows up. There’s something alive about the noise. It contains the ghost of every sentence you didn’t write, every idea you almost had, every tangent you chose not to take.

Maybe that’s why free writing feels so human. It lets us be multiple selves for a moment: the one who wants to be profound, the one who wants to be silly, the one who is secretly thinking about lunch. When we refuse to edit ourselves too quickly, we give those selves room to speak. And sometimes the most honest thing we can say is the thing we didn’t know we were thinking.

So here I am, writing freely, and I have no idea where this is going. I’m not even sure it has a point. But maybe that’s the point. We don’t always need to produce something useful. Sometimes we just need to produce something—to let the mind stretch, to let the words stumble, to let the noise exist before it becomes signal.

I think the world could use more of that. More idle doodling. More meandering conversations. More time spent doing things that don’t have a clear return on investment. Because creativity is not a machine that you switch on when you have a deadline. It’s a garden that needs fallow seasons. It needs weeds, and rain, and days when nothing seems to happen. And out of that apparent waste, something eventually grows—unexpected, odd, and entirely your own.

So if you’ve made it this far, thank you for reading my little walk. I hope you get a chance today to write something with no destination. Or to think something with no purpose. Or to just sit with the noise, and let it teach you what it knows.
